text: A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus. It takes Venus 243 Earth days to rotate once on its axis, but only 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun.
Neutron stars are so dense that a teaspoon of their material would weigh about 6 billion tons on Earth.
There is a giant cloud of alcohol in space — Sagittarius B2 contains enough ethyl alcohol to fill 400 trillion trillion pints of beer.
The footprints on the Moon will likely remain there for 100 million years because there is no wind or water to erode them.
India's Chandrayaan-1 mission in 2008 was the first to confirm water molecules on the Moon's surface.
There is a giant cloud of alcohol in space — Sagittarius B2 contains enough ethanol to fill 400 trillion trillion pints of beer.
The International Space Station travels at about 28,000 km/h, orbiting Earth roughly every 90 minutes.
Neutron stars can spin up to 716 times per second — faster than a kitchen blender.
China's Tiangong space station, completed in 2022, is the third crewed space station after Mir and the ISS.
The UAE's Hope probe, launched in 2020, made the country the first Arab nation to reach Mars orbit.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm that has been raging for at least 350 years — longer than any storm ever recorded on Earth.
Saturn's rings are made mostly of ice and rock and are only about 10 to 100 meters thick despite spanning up to 282,000 km across.
The Milky Way galaxy contains an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars, and our Sun is just one of them.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, traveling at 299,792 km per second.
The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on December 25, 2021, can observe galaxies formed just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.
Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system — Olympus Mons — which stands about 22 km high, nearly three times the height of Mount Everest.
The observable universe is estimated to be about 93 billion light-years in diameter, containing roughly 2 trillion galaxies.
Pluto's largest moon Charon is so big relative to Pluto that they orbit each other around a common point in space between them.
The Voyager 1 spacecraft, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object ever, now over 23 billion km from Earth.
Black holes don't suck — they have the same gravitational pull as a star of equal mass. Only objects that come very close are in danger.
Europa, one of Jupiter's moons, has a subsurface ocean beneath its icy crust that may contain twice as much liquid water as all of Earth's oceans combined.
ISRO's Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission), launched in 2013, made India the first nation to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt.
The Sun accounts for about 99.86% of all the mass in the entire solar system.
The Andromeda Galaxy is on a collision course with the Milky Way, expected to merge in about 4.5 billion years.
Space is completely silent because there is no medium for sound waves to travel through in a vacuum.
China's Chang'e 4 mission in January 2019 was the first spacecraft to land on the far side of the Moon.
Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is the only moon in the solar system with a dense atmosphere and liquid lakes — but they are filled with methane, not water.
The first gravitational waves were detected by LIGO on September 14, 2015 — confirming a prediction Albert Einstein made 100 years earlier.
Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft returned samples from asteroid Ryugu to Earth in December 2020, delivering pristine material from the early solar system.
Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe, yet it has never been directly detected — we only know it exists through its gravitational effects.
The hottest planet in our solar system is Venus, not Mercury, because its thick CO2 atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect.
The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, has made more than 1.5 million observations and helped determine the universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
Uranus rotates on its side with an axial tilt of 98 degrees, meaning it essentially rolls around the Sun like a bowling ball.
The European Space Agency's Rosetta spacecraft became the first mission to orbit a comet when it arrived at Comet 67P in 2014.
One million Earths could fit inside the Sun, and the Sun itself is considered a medium-sized star compared to giants like UY Scuti.
The first image of a black hole — the supermassive black hole in galaxy M87 — was captured by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.
Enceladus, a small moon of Saturn, sprays water vapor and ice particles into space from geysers near its south pole, hinting at a subsurface ocean.
The Parker Solar Probe, launched in 2018, has flown closer to the Sun than any spacecraft in history, entering the solar corona.
Neptune's largest moon Triton orbits backwards compared to Neptune's rotation, suggesting it was captured from the Kuiper Belt long ago.
Russia's Sputnik 1, launched on October 4, 1957, was the world's first artificial satellite, triggering the Space Age and the Space Race.
The cosmic microwave background radiation is the leftover thermal radiation from the Big Bang, filling the entire observable universe uniformly.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on April 12, 1961, completing a single orbit of Earth aboard the Soviet Vostok 1 spacecraft.
The asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter contains millions of rocky objects, but their total mass is less than 4% of the Moon's mass.
NASA's Perseverance rover successfully produced oxygen on Mars in 2021 using the MOXIE instrument, a key step toward future crewed missions.
Space weather from solar flares and coronal mass ejections can disrupt GPS satellites, power grids, and radio communications on Earth.
The Kuiper Belt, a region of icy bodies beyond Neptune, is home to Pluto and may contain hundreds of thousands of objects larger than 100 km.
Exoplanet WASP-12b is so close to its host star that it is being torn apart by tidal forces and will be completely destroyed within 3 million years.
The Crab Nebula is the remnant of a supernova explosion observed by Chinese and Arab astronomers in 1054 AD, now expanding at 1,500 km per second.
Japan's Akatsuki spacecraft, after a failed Venus orbit insertion in 2010, re-attempted in 2015 and became Japan's first successful planetary orbiter.
Io, Jupiter's innermost large moon, is the most volcanically active body in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes erupting continuously.
The Oort Cloud, a vast shell of icy objects surrounding the solar system, may extend up to 100,000 AU from the Sun — nearly halfway to the nearest star.
The first woman in space was Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova, who orbited Earth 48 times aboard Vostok 6 in June 1963.
SpaceX's Falcon 9 became the first orbital rocket to successfully land and re-fly its first stage, transforming the economics of spaceflight.
Dark energy, which makes up about 68% of the universe, is causing the expansion of the universe to accelerate — a discovery that won the 2011 Nobel Prize.
ESA's Gaia spacecraft has mapped the precise positions and motions of nearly 2 billion stars in the Milky Way, creating the most detailed galactic census ever.
A year on Mercury lasts only 88 Earth days, yet a single day on Mercury (sunrise to sunrise) lasts 176 Earth days — two Mercurian years.
The Perseid meteor shower occurs every August when Earth passes through debris left by Comet Swift-Tuttle, producing up to 100 meteors per hour.
India's Chandrayaan-3 successfully landed near the Moon's south pole in August 2023, making India the first nation to achieve a soft landing at that location.
The TRAPPIST-1 system, 39 light-years away, has seven Earth-sized planets, three of which sit in the habitable zone where liquid water could exist.
The Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way about 160,000 light-years away, is visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere.
China's Zhurong rover, part of the Tianwen-1 mission, landed on Mars in May 2021, making China only the second country to successfully operate a rover on Mars.
The Sun's core reaches temperatures of about 15 million degrees Celsius, where nuclear fusion converts hydrogen into helium and releases energy.
The Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula, made famous by Hubble, are columns of gas and dust that are 4 to 5 light-years tall — stellar nurseries.
Mars has the largest canyon in the solar system — Valles Marineris — stretching over 4,000 km long and up to 7 km deep.
White dwarf stars are incredibly dense remnants of dead stars — one teaspoon of white dwarf material would weigh about 15 tons on Earth.
Halley's Comet is visible from Earth roughly every 75 to 76 years; its last appearance was in 1986 and the next is expected around 2061.
NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto in July 2015, revealing mountains of water ice, a heart-shaped nitrogen plain, and a tenuous atmosphere.
ESA's Solar Orbiter mission, launched in 2020, has captured the closest-ever photographs of the Sun, revealing small-scale jet features called campfires.
The nearest star system to Earth, Alpha Centauri, is about 4.37 light-years away — so far that it would take over 70,000 years with current spacecraft.
The first Chinese taikonaut, Yang Liwei, flew to space on October 15, 2003, making China only the third country to independently send humans into orbit.
The Big Bang occurred approximately 13.8 billion years ago; for the first 380,000 years the universe was opaque, too hot for light to travel freely.
NASA's Curiosity rover, operating since 2012, confirmed that ancient Mars had liquid water and conditions potentially suitable for microbial life.
Quasars are the most luminous persistent objects in the universe — powered by supermassive black holes consuming material, they can outshine entire galaxies.
The Moon is gradually moving away from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 cm per year due to tidal interactions, and in the distant past it was much closer.
ISRO's Aditya-L1, launched in September 2023, is India's first solar observatory and studies the Sun from the Lagrange Point 1.
The Sagittarius A* black hole at the center of the Milky Way has a mass of about 4 million Suns, confirmed by the Event Horizon Telescope image in 2022.
All the elements heavier than iron in the universe — including gold and platinum — were forged in neutron star collisions called kilonovae.
The International Space Station has been continuously inhabited by humans since November 2, 2000, making it over two decades of uninterrupted human presence in space.
Saturn's moon Mimas has a massive crater called Herschel that makes it look remarkably like the Death Star from the Star Wars films.
Russia's Luna-9 became the first spacecraft to achieve a soft landing on the Moon in February 1966, transmitting the first photos from the lunar surface.
The Hubble constant — measuring how fast the universe is expanding — remains one of cosmology's biggest unsolved mysteries due to conflicting measurements.
The Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile, built by ESO, NRAO, and NAOJ, is the world's most powerful radio telescope array for studying cold cosmic dust.
Astronauts on the ISS experience about 16 sunrises and sunsets every 24 hours because of their 90-minute orbital period.
Betelgeuse, a red supergiant star in Orion, is so large that if placed at the center of our solar system, it would engulf everything out to Jupiter's orbit.
Japan's SLIM lander touched down on the Moon in January 2024, making Japan only the fifth country to achieve a lunar soft landing.
The total solar eclipse of August 2017 tracked across the continental United States, the first to do so since 1918.
The Fermi Bubbles are two enormous structures extending 25,000 light-years above and below the Milky Way's center, discovered by the Fermi Space Telescope in 2010.
The surface of the Moon reaches 127°C during the day and plunges to -173°C at night, an extreme range due to lack of insulating atmosphere.
Proxima Centauri b, an exoplanet orbiting our nearest stellar neighbor, sits in the habitable zone — but the star's violent flares may strip any atmosphere.
The heaviest element created entirely in stars by nuclear fusion is iron; elements heavier than iron require supernova explosions or neutron star mergers.
The Apollo 11 mission landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin becoming the first humans to walk on another world.
The Cassini spacecraft spent 13 years orbiting Saturn before deliberately plunging into the planet's atmosphere in 2017 to protect its moons from contamination.
Neptune's winds are the fastest in the solar system, reaching speeds of up to 2,100 km/h — despite being so far from the Sun's warming energy.
Cosmic rays are high-energy particles that constantly bombard Earth from outer space; the most energetic ones can carry more kinetic energy than a tennis ball.
ESA's Mars Express has been orbiting Mars since 2003, and in 2023 its radar confirmed a large deposit of water ice at the Martian south pole.
The Voyager probes carry a Golden Record with sounds and images of Earth, intended as a message to any extraterrestrial civilization that might find them.
The Boomerang Nebula, formed by a dying star, is the coldest known natural place in the universe at about -272°C — just one degree above absolute zero.
Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system, and its iron core makes up about 85% of its radius, giving it the second highest density after Earth.
India's first crewed spaceflight program, Gaganyaan, aims to send Indian astronauts to space aboard an indigenous spacecraft — a major milestone for ISRO.
Gamma-ray bursts are the most powerful explosions in the universe, releasing in seconds more energy than the Sun will emit in its entire 10-billion-year lifetime.
Jupiter has 95 known moons as of 2023, the most of any planet in the solar system — many are small irregular bodies captured from elsewhere.
The Milky Way's spiral arms, where most star formation occurs, take about 225 to 250 million years to complete one orbit — called a galactic year.
NASA's DART mission in 2022 deliberately crashed a spacecraft into asteroid Dimorphos and successfully altered its orbit — the first planetary defense test.
The Sloan Great Wall, a vast cosmic structure about 1.37 billion light-years long, is one of the largest known structures in the observable universe.
Astronauts on long-duration missions to the ISS experience bone density loss, muscle atrophy, and fluid shifts toward the head due to microgravity.
Mars has seasons similar to Earth's because it has an axial tilt of about 25 degrees, very close to Earth's 23.4 degrees.
The Chandra X-ray Observatory has observed the hottest and most energetic phenomena in the universe, including black holes, supernova remnants, and galaxy clusters.
China launched the world's first quantum communication satellite, Micius, in 2016, enabling experiments in quantum cryptography across thousands of kilometers.
The largest known star, Stephenson 2-18, has a radius about 2,150 times that of the Sun — if placed in our solar system, it would extend past Saturn's orbit.
Russia's Venera 9 probe in 1975 was the first spacecraft to transmit photos from the surface of Venus, showing a rocky landscape with sharp-edged slabs.
The Horsehead Nebula in Orion gets its distinctive shape from dense cold gas and dust blocking the light from the hot glowing gas behind it.
The solar system is located in the Orion Arm — a minor spiral arm of the Milky Way — about 26,000 light-years from the galactic center.
JAXA's Akari infrared telescope, launched in 2006, completed a full-sky survey in infrared light, cataloguing over 1.3 million celestial sources.
The Great Attractor is a gravitational anomaly pulling the Milky Way and millions of other galaxies toward a region 250 million light-years away.
A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation — they are so regular they were initially mistaken for alien signals.
The first Mars landing was achieved by NASA's Viking 1 on July 20, 1976, which also performed the first biological experiments on Martian soil.
Sunspot cycles last approximately 11 years and influence space weather, satellite drag, radio communications, and even Earth's climate to a small degree.
The cosmic web is the large-scale structure of the universe — a vast network of filaments of galaxies separated by enormous voids hundreds of millions of light-years across.
Water was first confirmed on Mars in the form of polar ice caps; liquid water may have flowed on Mars billions of years ago when it had a thicker atmosphere.
ESA's XMM-Newton X-ray telescope has discovered that galaxy clusters — the largest gravitationally bound objects — are filled with hot gas at millions of degrees.
Russia's Mir space station was occupied for 12 consecutive years from 1989 to 1999, setting records for long-duration human spaceflight.
The radio signal from Voyager 1, traveling at the speed of light, now takes over 22 hours to reach Earth — a testament to its incredible distance.
The Kepler Space Telescope, launched in 2009, discovered over 2,600 confirmed exoplanets by detecting the tiny dip in starlight when a planet transits its star.
ESA and JAXA's BepiColombo mission, launched in 2018, is the most comprehensive mission ever sent to Mercury and consists of two orbiters.
Ganymede, Jupiter's largest moon, is bigger than the planet Mercury and is the only moon in the solar system known to have its own magnetic field.
A magnetar is a type of neutron star with the strongest known magnetic field in the universe — trillions of times stronger than Earth's magnetic field.
South Korea's KARI launched its first domestically-built orbital rocket, Nuri (KSLV-II), in June 2022, making it the seventh country to do so independently.
The Lyman-alpha forest — a pattern of absorption lines in quasar spectra — allows astronomers to map the distribution of hydrogen gas in the early universe.
Saturn has 146 known moons as of 2023, including Titan and Enceladus — and dozens of newly discovered small irregular satellites.
The Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) precisely measured tiny temperature fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background, confirming the Big Bang model.
Asteroid 16 Psyche is estimated to contain enough iron and nickel to be worth an estimated $10 quintillion — more than Earth's entire economy. NASA sent an orbiter to study it.
The Pillars of Creation may actually already be gone — they are 6,500 light-years away, so we are seeing them as they were 6,500 years ago.
ESA's Planck satellite, retired in 2013, provided the most precise map ever made of the cosmic microwave background, refining our knowledge of the universe's age and composition.
The Arecibo Message was a radio broadcast sent from Puerto Rico toward globular cluster M13 in 1974 — it will take 25,000 years to arrive.
Blazars are a subtype of quasars with their relativistic jet pointed almost directly at Earth, making them among the brightest objects ever observed.
NASA's Ingenuity helicopter became the first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another planet when it flew on Mars in April 2021.
SpaceX's Starship, the world's most powerful rocket, completed its first successful test flight reaching space and splashing down in 2024.
The OSIRIS-REx mission returned a sample of asteroid Bennu to Earth in September 2023 — the largest asteroid sample ever retrieved.
The speed of light in a vacuum — 299,792,458 metres per second — is the absolute cosmic speed limit; no object with mass can reach it.
Japan's Hayabusa, launched in 2003, was the first mission to land on an asteroid and return a sample — from asteroid Itokawa — back to Earth in 2010.
The heliosphere is the vast bubble of solar wind extending far beyond the outer planets, shielding the solar system from interstellar cosmic rays.
General relativity predicts that massive objects curve spacetime; this was confirmed in 1919 when starlight was observed bending around the Sun during a solar eclipse.
Venus rotates in the opposite direction to most planets in the solar system, meaning on Venus the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.
The Spitzer Space Telescope, operating from 2003 to 2020, revolutionized infrared astronomy and helped discover TRAPPIST-1's seven Earth-like planets.
China's Yutu-2 rover, deployed by Chang'e 4, has been operating on the far side of the Moon longer than any other lunar rover in history.
The Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO), a joint ESA/NASA mission, has been watching the Sun since 1995 and has discovered over 4,000 comets.
Tidal locking causes the Moon to always show the same face to Earth — its rotation period equals its orbital period of 27.3 days.
The Coriolis effect from Earth's rotation shapes cyclones and other large atmospheric patterns, but in space stations without atmosphere it has no weather effects.
Russia's Mars 3 probe in December 1971 was the first spacecraft to achieve a soft landing on Mars, transmitting a signal for 20 seconds before going silent.
The coldest place in the solar system is not Pluto but the shadowed craters near the Moon's poles, where temperatures can reach -240°C.
The discovery of water ice at the Moon's south pole by Chandrayaan-1 and LCROSS has sparked global interest in lunar resource utilization for future bases.
The Triangulum Galaxy (M33), 2.7 million light-years away, is the most distant object visible to the naked eye under ideal dark sky conditions.
Type Ia supernovae are used as cosmic standard candles to measure distances in the universe, and their observations led to the discovery of dark energy in 1998.
ESA's Venus Express mission, which orbited Venus from 2006 to 2014, confirmed strong evidence of active volcanism on Venus's surface.
The gas giant Jupiter acts as a gravitational shield for Earth, its massive gravity deflecting or capturing many asteroids and comets that might otherwise strike the inner solar system.
Astronaut Scott Kelly spent 340 days continuously on the ISS in 2015-2016; comparison with his twin brother showed genetic expression changes from spaceflight.
Titan is the only body other than Earth known to have stable liquid lakes and rivers on its surface — though they are filled with liquid methane and ethane.
The Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy is slowly merging into the Milky Way — some of the stars in the Milky Way's disk are believed to originate from this absorbed galaxy.
The Soviet Lunokhod 1, deployed in 1970, was the first remote-controlled rover ever to operate on another world, traveling 10.5 km on the Moon.
A solar wind composed of charged particles streams constantly from the Sun at 400–800 km/s, reaching all the way to the outer solar system.
The auroras (northern and southern lights) are caused by charged particles from the Sun interacting with Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere.
The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, launched in 2009, has created the most detailed maps of the Moon ever made, identifying ideal landing sites for future missions.
Interstellar object 'Oumuamua, detected in 2017, was the first confirmed interstellar object to pass through our solar system — shaped like a cigar and accelerating unusually.
The European Southern Observatory's Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) in Chile, when completed, will be the world's largest optical/infrared telescope with a 39-metre mirror.
Liquid metallic hydrogen inside Jupiter generates the planet's powerful magnetic field — the strongest magnetic field of any planet in the solar system.
Methane (CH4) has been detected in Mars's atmosphere in seasonal pulses, hinting at possible biological or geological subsurface activity.
China's Chang'e 5 mission returned 1.73 kg of lunar samples to Earth in December 2020 — the first such samples collected since the Soviet Luna 24 mission in 1976.
Binary star systems — two stars orbiting each other — are actually very common; over half of Sun-like stars are estimated to have a stellar companion.
NASA's Artemis I mission in 2022 sent the Orion capsule around the Moon and back as an uncrewed test flight, setting the stage for returning humans to the Moon.
Phosphine was controversially detected in the atmosphere of Venus in 2020, sparking debate about whether biological processes could exist in its acidic clouds.
Russia's Venera 7, in December 1970, was the first spacecraft to successfully transmit data from the surface of another planet.
The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), planned for launch in the 2030s, will be a space-based gravitational wave detector using three spacecraft in a triangle millions of kilometres apart.
The Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) satellite won its team the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics after detecting the first tiny anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background.
ESA's Herschel Space Observatory, active from 2009 to 2013, detected water vapour venting from Ceres in the asteroid belt, suggesting icy interiors.
The Coma Cluster, about 320 million light-years away, contains over 1,000 galaxies and was the first evidence of dark matter proposed by Fritz Zwicky in 1933.
Cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov holds the record for the longest single spaceflight: 437 days aboard the Mir space station in 1994–95.
The Wide Field Infrared Survey Telescope (Roman Space Telescope), planned for the 2020s, will survey the sky 1,000 times faster than Hubble at the same depth.
The Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, is mysteriously hotter than its surface — reaching millions of degrees compared to just 5,500°C at the photosphere.
ISRO's PSLV rocket has launched over 400 foreign satellites for 34 countries, making India one of the world's most cost-effective commercial launch service providers.
The first detection of gravitational waves from two merging neutron stars, in 2017, also produced visible light — inaugurating the era of multi-messenger astronomy.
The Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect describes how cosmic microwave background photons are distorted by hot gas in galaxy clusters, revealing them across the universe.
The New Horizons probe discovered that Arrokoth — the most distant object ever visited by a spacecraft — is a contact binary, two lobes gently merged together.
Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt, is classified as a dwarf planet and was the first object to be visited by a spacecraft in the asteroid belt (NASA's Dawn, 2015).
The ESA/NASA Ulysses mission was the first to study the Sun's poles, flying over both the north and south poles and measuring the solar wind in three dimensions.
Russia and the US have operated joint missions since the Apollo-Soyuz docking in 1975 — a handshake in space that symbolised détente between the superpowers.
Triton is geologically active, with nitrogen geysers erupting from its south polar region — driven by solar heating of sub-surface nitrogen ice.
The hydrogen and helium that make up most of the universe were produced in the first few minutes after the Big Bang in a process called Big Bang nucleosynthesis.
China's FAST (Five-hundred-metre Aperture Spherical Telescope), completed in 2016, is the world's largest single-dish radio telescope, spanning 500 metres.
Cosmic inflation — a brief period of exponential expansion fractions of a second after the Big Bang — explains why the observable universe appears so uniform.
The first satellite from South Asia was India's Aryabhata, launched by the Soviet Union for ISRO on April 19, 1975, marking India's entry into the Space Age.
The twin GRACE satellites measured tiny changes in Earth's gravity to track melting ice sheets, groundwater depletion, and sea level rise from space.
Tidal locking of Pluto and Charon means both bodies always show the same face to each other — they orbit their common center of mass like a double dwarf planet.
Juno, which has been orbiting Jupiter since 2016, revealed that Jupiter's storms extend thousands of kilometres deep into its atmosphere, far deeper than expected.
The European Geostationary Navigation Overlay Service (EGNOS) and Galileo satellite system provide independent GPS-like navigation for Europe's infrastructure and aviation.
The first interstellar comet ever observed, Borisov, was discovered in 2019 and found to be largely unchanged, composed of pristine material from another star system.
JAXA's IKAROS spacecraft, launched in 2010, was the first operational solar sail in space, using sunlight pressure for propulsion beyond Earth's orbit.
Stellar parallax — the apparent shift of nearby stars against distant background stars as Earth orbits the Sun — was the first direct proof that Earth moves around the Sun.
Russia's Spektr-RG space telescope, launched in 2019, has completed the deepest full-sky X-ray survey ever, mapping over 1 million X-ray sources across the universe.
Brown dwarfs are objects too massive to be planets but too small to sustain nuclear fusion like stars — often called failed stars, they glow faintly in infrared.
The Andromeda Galaxy, the Milky Way, and more than 54 other galaxies form the Local Group — a gravitationally bound cluster spanning about 10 million light-years.
An AU (Astronomical Unit) is the average distance from Earth to the Sun — about 150 million km — and is the standard unit for measuring distances within the solar system.
The Subaru Telescope on Mauna Kea, operated by NAOJ (Japan), is one of the world's largest optical telescopes and has discovered some of the most distant known galaxies.
Phobos, the larger of Mars's two moons, is spiraling inward and will either crash into Mars or break apart into a ring system in about 50 million years.
The Stardust mission, launched in 1999, collected dust particles from Comet Wild 2 and returned them to Earth in 2006 — the first comet material ever returned.
The afterglow of the most powerful gamma-ray burst ever recorded, GRB 221009A in 2022, was so bright it briefly overwhelmed detectors on several space observatories.
The Moon formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago when a Mars-sized body called Theia collided with the early Earth, ejecting debris that coalesced into the Moon.
The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, a joint ESA-Roscosmos mission, has been mapping trace gases in Mars's atmosphere since 2018 and found surprising hydrogen chloride.
The James Webb Space Telescope discovered carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of WASP-39b, the first clear detection of CO2 in an exoplanet's atmosphere.
China's BeiDou navigation satellite system became fully operational in 2020, offering global coverage as an alternative to GPS — the third global navigation system after GPS and GLONASS.

The Virgo Supercluster — our cosmic neighborhood — contains the Local Group plus dozens of other galaxy groups, spanning about 110 million light-years, yet is itself just a tendril of the larger Laniakea Supercluster.
Callisto, Jupiter's outermost Galilean moon, is the most heavily cratered object in the solar system — its ancient surface has not been resurfaced by geological activity for billions of years.

Amalthea, Jupiter's third-closest moon, is so small and dark that it absorbs nearly all the sunlight that hits it, yet radiates more heat than it receives — likely because it is heated by Jupiter's magnetic field.
Saturn's moon Hyperion is the largest known irregularly shaped moon in the solar system, tumbling chaotically in its orbit rather than rotating steadily.
Phoebe, a distant moon of Saturn, orbits in the opposite direction to most of Saturn's moons and is believed to be a captured Kuiper Belt object rather than a body that formed with Saturn.
Ariel, one of Uranus's moons, has the brightest and youngest surface of any Uranian moon, with vast fault valleys and plains resurfaced by flows of icy material.
Miranda, Uranus's smallest and innermost major moon, has Verona Rupes — a cliff face up to 20 km tall, possibly the tallest known cliff in the solar system.
Sirius, the brightest star in Earth's night sky, is actually a binary system: Sirius A is a white main-sequence star orbited by Sirius B, a dense white dwarf.
Algol in the constellation Perseus is a famous eclipsing binary — its brightness dips every 2.87 days as the dimmer companion passes in front of the brighter star.
PSR J0437-4715 is the closest and brightest millisecond pulsar to Earth, spinning 174 times per second and serving as an ultra-precise natural clock used to test general relativity.
SGR 1806-20, a magnetar located 50,000 light-years away, released a giant flare in December 2004 that briefly outshone the full Moon at gamma-ray energies and ionised part of Earth's ionosphere.
The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) detector, buried 1,480 metres underground in South Dakota, is the world's most sensitive dark matter detector, using 10 tonnes of liquid xenon.

The XENONnT experiment at the Gran Sasso laboratory in Italy searches for weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) — leading dark matter candidates — using ultra-pure liquid xenon shielded from cosmic rays.
There are an estimated 27,000 pieces of orbital debris larger than 10 cm tracked by the US Space Surveillance Network — with millions of smaller untracked fragments also circling Earth.
The Kessler Syndrome, proposed by NASA scientist Donald Kessler in 1978, describes a cascade where collisions between debris generate more debris, potentially making low Earth orbit unusable.
The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, signed by over 110 nations, prohibits placing nuclear weapons in orbit, claims of sovereignty over celestial bodies, and military installations on the Moon.
The Artemis Accords, established by NASA in 2020 and signed by over 40 nations, set norms for peaceful, transparent, and sustainable exploration of the Moon and beyond.
The Moon Agreement of 1979, which declares the Moon and its resources as the common heritage of mankind, has been ratified by fewer than 20 countries and not by any major spacefaring nation.
Astronauts on the ISS eat specially packaged thermostabilised, freeze-dried, and irradiated foods; some fresh fruits and vegetables arrive on resupply missions as a morale-boosting treat.
NASA's Advanced Plant Habitat on the ISS successfully grew red romaine lettuce in 2015, with astronauts tasting space-grown food for the first time as part of the VEGGIE experiment.
Spacewalks — officially called EVAs (extravehicular activities) — typically last 6–8 hours; astronauts pre-breathe pure oxygen for hours beforehand to prevent decompression sickness.
Alexei Leonov performed the first spacewalk on March 18, 1965, spending 12 minutes outside his Voskhod 2 spacecraft — nearly unable to re-enter because his suit had inflated too rigidly.

Perseverance rover carries 23 cameras and a microphone, making it the first Mars rover to record audio on the Red Planet — capturing the sounds of Martian wind and the rotors of the Ingenuity helicopter.
Perseverance is caching rock and soil samples in sealed tubes on the Martian surface for potential retrieval by a future Mars Sample Return mission, planned as a joint NASA-ESA effort.
Curiosity rover discovered boron in Martian rocks in 2016 — a sign that ancient Mars may have had long-lived groundwater, because boron is only left behind when water evaporates slowly.
China's Zhurong rover detected evidence of ancient flood events on the southern Utopia Planitia plain of Mars, suggesting liquid water once shaped the region's geology.
ESA's EnVision mission, planned for launch in the early 2030s, will study Venus's surface, subsurface, and atmosphere in unprecedented detail to understand why it became so hostile.
NASA's DAVINCI mission will drop a probe through Venus's atmosphere in the late 2020s to sample its gases directly, revealing clues about how Venus evolved so differently from Earth.
NASA's VERITAS mission will map Venus's entire surface in high resolution radar to determine whether it is geologically active today, building on limited data from the Magellan mission of the 1990s.
MESSENGER, the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury, confirmed in 2012 that water ice exists in permanently shadowed craters near Mercury's poles despite the planet's proximity to the Sun.
Mercury has a global magnetic field despite its small size and slow rotation — a surprising finding from the Mariner 10 flyby in 1974 that still challenges theories of planetary dynamos.

Asteroid mining company Planetary Resources (founded 2012) and Deep Space Industries were early commercial ventures aiming to extract water and metals from asteroids, though both were later acquired or dissolved.

Water extracted from near-Earth asteroids could be split into hydrogen and oxygen for rocket propellant, potentially creating fuel depots in space that drastically cut the cost of deep-space missions.
Virgin Galactic's VSS Unity became the first commercial spaceflight to carry paying passengers to the edge of space in 2023, briefly reaching above 80 km — NASA's definition of the space boundary.
Blue Origin's New Shepard rocket has carried paying space tourists on suborbital hops since 2021, with Jeff Bezos himself on the first crewed flight on July 20, 2021.
The L4 and L5 Lagrange points in the Earth-Sun system are stable gravitational sweet spots 60 degrees ahead of and behind Earth in its orbit, and are proposed sites for future space settlements.
The James Webb Space Telescope orbits the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point, 1.5 million km from Earth on the night side, where its sunshield can permanently block the Sun, Earth, and Moon simultaneously.
Jupiter's L4 and L5 Lagrange points host the Trojan asteroids — over 10,000 asteroids that share Jupiter's orbit, roughly 60 degrees ahead and behind the planet.
NASA's Lucy mission, launched in 2021, will fly by eight Trojan asteroids over 12 years — the most diverse asteroid tour ever attempted — to study these primordial remnants of the early solar system.

Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays with energies above 10^20 electron volts — called Oh-My-God particles — are so rare and energetic that they should be absorbed by the cosmic microwave background before reaching Earth.

The Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina, covering 3,000 km², is the world's largest cosmic ray detector, using over 1,600 water tanks and fluorescence telescopes to catch the rare showers from ultra-energetic particles.
Long gamma-ray bursts, lasting more than two seconds, are caused by the collapse of massive rotating stars into black holes — the most powerful known explosions in the universe since the Big Bang.
Short gamma-ray bursts, lasting less than two seconds, result from the merger of two neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole — and are a key source of heavy elements like gold.
Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio flashes from extragalactic distances; the first was discovered in archival data in 2007 and the source of most remains unexplained.
In 2020, astronomers traced a repeating fast radio burst (FRB 20200120E) to a globular cluster in a nearby galaxy — evidence that at least some FRBs are produced by magnetars.
LIGO and Virgo have detected over 90 gravitational wave events, mostly from merging black holes and neutron stars, revealing a previously hidden population of compact objects in the universe.

KAGRA, Japan's cryogenically cooled gravitational wave detector inside a mountain, joined LIGO and Virgo in 2020 as part of a global network to triangulate the sky positions of gravitational wave sources.
The Webb telescope's NIRCam instrument can detect the heat signature of a bumblebee at the distance of the Moon, illustrating its extraordinary infrared sensitivity.
The Hubble Space Telescope's Deep Field images, taken in 1995 and 2004, revealed thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky previously thought nearly empty — forever changing our view of the universe.
Chandra X-ray Observatory discovered that the Perseus galaxy cluster rings like a bell — sound waves from its central black hole create ripples in the hot gas visible only in X-rays.
NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope detected the first light from an exoplanet in 2005 by measuring the slight dimming when the planet moved behind its star — a technique called secondary eclipse.

NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope discovered an unexplained excess of gamma rays from the Milky Way's center — a signal consistent with dark matter annihilation, though the cause remains debated.
The interstellar medium (ISM) — the gas and dust filling the space between stars — makes up about 10–15% of the Milky Way's total mass and is where new stars are born.
The ISM contains three main phases: hot ionized gas, warm neutral or ionized gas, and cold molecular clouds — with vastly different temperatures and densities coexisting across the galaxy.

Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) — complex organic molecules — are abundant throughout the interstellar medium and may have contributed the raw chemical building blocks for life on early Earth.
The Crab Pulsar at the heart of the Crab Nebula spins 30 times per second and powers the nebula's glow by converting rotational energy into electromagnetic radiation and fast particles.
Millisecond pulsars are thought to be 'recycled' — old neutron stars spun up to extremely fast rotation rates by accreting matter from a companion star over millions of years.
The pulsar timing array technique uses dozens of millisecond pulsars as a galaxy-sized gravitational wave detector, and in 2023 multiple teams announced evidence of a gravitational wave background.

Alpha Centauri A and B form a binary pair orbiting each other every 79 years, while Proxima Centauri — a red dwarf — orbits this pair at a far greater distance, completing one orbit in roughly 550,000 years.
Eta Carinae is a luminous blue hypergiant binary system about 7,500 light-years away; it experienced a giant eruption in the 1840s and is a candidate for one of the Milky Way's next supernovae.
W Ursae Majoris is a contact binary star — both stars share a common outer envelope and are so close they merge into an oval shape, losing mass from their shared surface.
ESA's Euclid telescope, launched in 2023, will map the 3D positions of over 1.5 billion galaxies across 10 billion years of cosmic history to measure the effects of dark energy and dark matter.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, beginning full operations around 2025, will image the entire southern sky every three nights for 10 years — creating the most complete census of the dynamic universe ever made.
Low Earth orbit is cluttered enough that the ISS has had to perform more than 30 debris avoidance maneuvers since 1999, using its thrusters to dodge tracked pieces of space junk.
Japan's ELSA-d satellite, launched in 2021, demonstrated a magnetic capture system for deorbiting space debris — the first active debris removal technology test in orbit.
The UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) has been the primary international body governing space activities since 1959, overseeing the drafting of major space law treaties.
Astronaut food in the 1960s included squeeze tubes of pureed food; by the Apollo program, astronauts ate bite-sized cubes and freeze-dried food they rehydrated with water from the fuel cell.
Pizza has been delivered to the ISS via Progress resupply vehicles — Russian cosmonauts have been known to receive tinned salmon, cheese, and fresh onions as special dietary items.
The longest spacewalk on record lasted 8 hours and 56 minutes, performed by Susan Helms and Jim Voss in March 2001 to rearrange a docking port on the ISS.

NASA's Manned Maneuvering Unit (MMU), used on three Shuttle missions in 1984, allowed astronauts to fly untethered up to 100 metres from the Shuttle — the only time humans have flown truly free in open space.

Catharina Villalpando-Donahue, a researcher at NASA's Johnson Space Center, helped develop the current ISS spacesuit (EMU) — it has 14 layers of materials designed to protect against micrometeorites, temperature extremes, and radiation.
Perseverance rover confirmed the ancient delta in Jezero Crater once carried water into a lake, preserving organic molecules in sedimentary rock — the best candidate site for fossilised Martian life.
Curiosity rover has driven over 30 km on Mars since 2012 and climbed the lower slopes of Mount Sharp (Aeolis Mons), reading billions of years of Martian geological history in its rock layers.
China's Zhurong rover found widespread evidence of frost and a water-cycle process in Utopia Planitia, suggesting liquid brines may still form briefly on Mars today during cold seasons.

The ISM contains a Local Bubble — a roughly spherical cavity about 1,000 light-years across around our solar system, carved out by supernova explosions millions of years ago and filled with hot, low-density gas.
Gravitational lensing — where a massive galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from more distant galaxies behind it — has allowed astronomers to observe objects far too faint to see directly.

The Bullet Cluster is the most famous evidence for dark matter: the hot X-ray-emitting gas of two colliding galaxy clusters was slowed by pressure, but the dark matter passed straight through, creating a separation visible to Chandra.
NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in October 2024, will fly by Jupiter's moon Europa 49 times to assess the habitability of its subsurface ocean, searching for the chemical ingredients for life.
ESA's JUICE (Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer) mission, launched in April 2023, will orbit Ganymede in 2034 — the first spacecraft ever to orbit a moon other than Earth's Moon.

Dragonfly, NASA's rotorcraft lander mission to Titan, will fly to dozens of sites across the moon's surface after a planned 2028 launch, searching for prebiotic chemistry in its methane seas and dunes.
The Voyager 1 probe crossed the heliopause — the boundary where the solar wind gives way to interstellar space — in August 2012, becoming the first human-made object in true interstellar space.

GW150914, the first detected gravitational wave event, came from two black holes — one of 36 solar masses and one of 29 — merging 1.3 billion light-years away and radiating three solar masses of pure energy in under a second.
The Andromeda Galaxy contains a double nucleus — two bright clumps near its center — believed to be a single black hole surrounded by an eccentric disk of old stars rather than two separate nuclei.
The Chandra Deep Field South is the longest cumulative X-ray image ever taken — 7 million seconds of exposure — revealing thousands of black holes in the early universe.
The Fermi paradox asks: given the high probability of extraterrestrial civilizations existing, why have we found no evidence of them? It remains one of the deepest unsolved questions in science.

The 72-second 'Wow! signal' recorded at the Big Ear radio telescope in 1977 remains the strongest candidate signal for extraterrestrial intelligence ever detected — it has never been confirmed or repeated.
Webb's first deep field image, released in July 2022, showed thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky smaller than a grain of sand held at arm's length — some dating back more than 13 billion years.
Hubble discovered that nearly every large galaxy harbours a supermassive black hole at its core, and the black hole's mass is closely linked to the mass of the surrounding stellar bulge.
The INTEGRAL (INTErnational Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory) satellite, an ESA mission launched in 2002, has been mapping gamma-ray sources across the Milky Way for over two decades.
Space tourism company Axiom Space has contracted NASA to build private modules attached to the ISS, eventually becoming a standalone commercial space station after the ISS is deorbited.
Lunar Gateway, the international space station planned for lunar orbit, will serve as a staging post for Artemis lunar landings and eventually as a hub for deep space exploration beyond the Moon.
Deimos, the smaller of Mars's two moons, measures only about 15 km across and is so small that a person could throw a baseball fast enough to escape its gravity and reach orbit.
Oberon, Uranus's outermost major moon, has a mountain at least 11 km tall on its limb — photographed by Voyager 2 in 1986 in the only close look humanity has had at the Uranian moons.
Dactyl, discovered in 1993 during the Galileo spacecraft's flyby, was the first known moon of an asteroid — orbiting the main-belt asteroid Ida at about 90 km distance.

Charon's large size relative to Pluto means the two bodies never face the same hemisphere toward each other — both are tidally locked so the same faces permanently point at each other across their shared barycenter.

The Webb telescope revealed that six massive galaxies existed just 500–700 million years after the Big Bang — far larger and more developed than models predicted, challenging standard galaxy formation theories.

Neutron stars have a surface gravity about 200 billion times stronger than Earth's — if you dropped a marshmallow from one metre above a neutron star, it would hit the surface with the energy of a nuclear bomb.
The cosmic ray flux reaching Earth is about 1,000 particles per square metre per second at sea level; most are protons and helium nuclei accelerated in supernovae or other energetic events.

The IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole, embedded in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, detected the first high-energy neutrinos from outside our galaxy — traced to an active galactic nucleus called TXS 0506+056.

Space debris collision velocities in low Earth orbit average about 10 km/s — a tiny paint flake at that speed carries enough energy to damage a spacecraft window, as seen on multiple Space Shuttle missions.

Russia's anti-satellite missile test in November 2021 destroyed its own Cosmos 1408 satellite, creating over 1,500 trackable debris pieces that forced ISS crews to shelter in docked spacecraft for hours.
Umbriel, the darkest of Uranus's large moons, has a mysterious bright ring-shaped feature called the Wunda crater on its dark face — its origin remains unexplained.
Titania, the largest moon of Uranus, has a 1,600 km long canyon called Messina Chasmata that formed as the moon's interior expanded and cracked its icy crust during cooling.

Proteus, one of Neptune's inner moons discovered by Voyager 2 in 1989, is so dark it reflects only 6% of the light that hits it — nearly as black as soot — making it nearly invisible to ground-based telescopes.

Nereid, Neptune's third-largest moon, has one of the most eccentric orbits of any moon in the solar system — its distance from Neptune varies from 1.4 million to 9.7 million km throughout its 360-day orbit.

Arp 220, the nearest ultraluminous infrared galaxy at 250 million light-years, is the product of two merging spiral galaxies and shines 1 trillion times brighter than the Sun due to intense star formation.

Theia Lacus on Titan — a dark equatorial lake roughly the size of Lake Superior — is filled with liquid methane and ethane and experiences methane rainstorms in a hydrological cycle analogous to Earth's water cycle.

The Atacama Cosmology Telescope in Chile has mapped the cosmic microwave background at finer resolution than any previous experiment, confirming the Standard Model of cosmology while hinting at tension in the Hubble constant.

The Square Kilometre Array (SKA), under construction in South Africa and Australia, will be the world's largest radio telescope when complete — sensitive enough to detect an airport radar on a planet 50 light-years away.

Exoplanet K2-18b, 120 light-years away, has been identified as a possible 'Hycean world' — a planet with a hydrogen-rich atmosphere and a liquid water ocean — with Webb detecting the molecule dimethyl sulfide, a potential biosignature.

TOI 700d, discovered by NASA's TESS mission, is a roughly Earth-sized planet in the habitable zone of a nearby red dwarf star just 100 light-years away — one of the most promising nearby potentially habitable worlds.
TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) has identified over 7,000 candidate exoplanets since launching in 2018, surveying nearly the entire sky in a two-year prime mission.

Hot Jupiters — gas giants orbiting extremely close to their stars in days or hours — were the first exoplanets discovered by the radial velocity method and surprised astronomers as nothing like our solar system.

Rogue planets — free-floating planets ejected from their star systems — may outnumber stars in the Milky Way; the Roman Space Telescope is expected to detect thousands of them using gravitational microlensing.

The habitable zone around a star — sometimes called the 'Goldilocks zone' — is the range of distances where liquid water could exist on a rocky planet's surface, and its boundaries depend on stellar luminosity and atmosphere.
The first exoplanet orbiting a sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, was discovered in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz — work that earned them the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Axion Dark Matter eXperiment (ADMX) at the University of Washington searches for axions — a hypothetical low-mass particle — using a microwave cavity resonator inside a powerful magnetic field.

A nanosat called LightSail 2, operated by The Planetary Society, demonstrated sustained solar-sail propulsion in Earth orbit in 2019 — proving the technology works for future low-cost deep space missions.
NASA's Lunar Flashlight CubeSat, launched in 2022, was intended to use laser reflectometry to map water ice on the Moon's surface — though a propulsion anomaly prevented it reaching lunar orbit.

India's NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) regional satellite navigation system became fully operational in 2018, providing positioning services to the Indian subcontinent and surrounding region.

The cosmic distance ladder is a succession of overlapping methods — parallax, Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae — used to measure ever greater distances in the universe, each calibrated by the previous rung.

Cepheid variable stars pulsate at rates directly linked to their intrinsic luminosity — a relationship discovered by Henrietta Swan Leavitt in 1908, enabling the measurement of extragalactic distances.
Stellar winds from massive O-type and B-type stars blow away their surrounding gas and dust clouds, sometimes quenching star formation in their region and shaping the structure of entire galaxies.
Magnetar SGR 1935+2154 produced a radio burst detectable from within the Milky Way in 2020 — confirming for the first time that at least some fast radio bursts are generated by magnetars.

Pulsar PSR B1919+21, the first pulsar ever detected, was discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish; its regular 1.33-second pulse was so perfect it was nicknamed LGM-1 (Little Green Men 1).
A double pulsar system, PSR J0737-3039A/B, discovered in 2003, provides the most stringent tests of general relativity ever performed — the two neutron stars orbit each other every 2.4 hours.
R136a1 in the Large Magellanic Cloud is estimated to be the most massive star known — potentially over 200 solar masses — and is 8.7 million times more luminous than the Sun.
Wolf-Rayet stars are massive, extremely hot stars in a late evolutionary stage that shed their outer envelopes through fierce stellar winds, enriching the interstellar medium with heavy elements.
NASA's proposed Interstellar Probe mission would launch on a Solar Gravity Assist trajectory, using the Sun as a gravitational lens to observe exoplanet atmospheres and reach 1,000 AU over 50 years.
The Allen Telescope Array (ATA) in California, used by the SETI Institute, is a 42-dish radio array dedicated partly to searching for technosignatures from extraterrestrial civilizations.

Breakthrough Listen, the largest scientific SETI programme ever funded, scans millions of stars and nearby galaxies for radio and laser signals using major telescopes including the Green Bank Telescope.
GN-z11, a galaxy observed by Hubble and confirmed by Webb, existed just 430 million years after the Big Bang and is one of the earliest and most distant galaxies ever studied.
MACS0647-JD, magnified by the galaxy cluster MACS0647, is one of the earliest known objects at a look-back time of 13.3 billion years — Webb resolved it into two distinct clumps of stars.
The Cosmic Origins Spectrograph on Hubble has mapped the cosmic web's 'missing' baryons — ordinary matter in hot filaments between galaxy clusters — solving the decades-old 'missing baryon problem'.

Jupiter's moon Europa is tidally heated by Jupiter's gravity, keeping its subsurface ocean liquid despite being five times farther from the Sun than Earth — the same tidal mechanism that makes Io volcanic.
Saturn's moon Dione has wispy streaks on its trailing hemisphere — actually a network of bright ice cliffs formed by tectonic fractures, imaged in detail by the Cassini spacecraft.

Saturn's moon Rhea may have a very thin oxygen atmosphere formed when charged particles from Saturn's magnetosphere split water ice on its surface — making it only the second body after Earth with a confirmed oxygen atmosphere.
Janus and Epimetheus are two of Saturn's small inner moons that share nearly the same orbit — every four years they swap orbital positions in a gravitational dance unique in the solar system.
Pan, one of Saturn's tiny shepherd moons, orbits within the Encke Gap of Saturn's A ring and has a distinctive flying-saucer shape caused by ring material accreting around its equator.

The Planetary Protection Policy requires NASA and other space agencies to sterilize spacecraft visiting potentially habitable worlds to prevent contamination of those environments with Earth microbes.

The Liability Convention of 1972 establishes that a launching state is absolutely liable for damage its spacecraft causes on Earth's surface — Canada invoked it after the Soviet Cosmos 954 satellite scattered nuclear debris over Canada in 1978.
The US Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015 was the first national law to grant private companies the right to own resources extracted from asteroids and other celestial bodies.
The Beresheet lunar lander, built by Israeli non-profit SpaceIL, became the first private spacecraft to attempt a lunar landing in April 2019, crashing due to a computer reset during descent.
Intuitive Machines' IM-1 lander (Nova-C) became the first US spacecraft to land on the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972, touching down near the lunar south pole in February 2024 — tilted but functional.
Pluto has five known moons — Charon, Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra — the four smaller ones likely formed from the same collision that created Charon.
Haumea, a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, spins so fast (once every 3.9 hours) that it is stretched into an egg shape and has a thin ring — the first ring system found around a dwarf planet.

Makemake, the second-brightest Kuiper Belt dwarf planet after Pluto, has no global atmosphere and a surface covered in frozen methane — conditions that keep it among the coldest bodies in the solar system.
Eris, a distant dwarf planet more massive than Pluto, triggered Pluto's reclassification in 2006 — its discovery by Mike Brown forced the IAU to redefine the word 'planet'.
Sedna, discovered in 2003, has the most distant known orbit of any object in our solar system — its closest approach to the Sun is 76 AU and it may take up to 11,400 years to complete one orbit.
The gravitational waves detected from GW170817 — a neutron star merger — arrived 1.7 seconds before its gamma-ray burst, confirming that gravitational waves and light travel at the same speed.

The Einstein Telescope, a proposed underground triangular gravitational wave observatory in Europe, would be 10 km on each side and sensitive enough to detect events throughout most of the observable universe.

Astronauts need roughly 2,700 calories per day on the ISS, slightly less than on Earth because lower activity and fluid shifts reduce caloric needs — but they must be protein-rich to counteract muscle loss.

Edamame, macha-flavoured rice crackers, and miso soup in sealed pouches have been part of JAXA astronauts' menus aboard the ISS — reflecting cultural food preferences as space food becomes more personalised.

In microgravity, taste and smell are reduced because bodily fluids shift towards the head, causing nasal congestion similar to a cold — which is one reason astronauts often prefer stronger-flavoured foods in space.
Peggy Whitson holds the US record for total cumulative spacewalking time at over 60 hours across 10 EVAs, and was also the oldest woman to fly to space when she launched at age 56.
China's taikonauts completed their first spacewalk together outside Tiangong space station in November 2022, marking a major milestone in China's human spaceflight programme.

The Canadarm2 robotic arm on the ISS, built by the Canadian Space Agency, moves along the exterior of the station on rails and has been essential to over 200 spacewalks — acting as a safety anchor and tool platform.
Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, studied by ESA's Rosetta mission, has a shape like a rubber duck because two separate cometesimals gently merged in the early solar system.

ESA's Philae lander, deployed from Rosetta in 2014, was the first spacecraft to land on a comet nucleus — it bounced twice before coming to rest in a shadowy spot where its solar panels could not charge.

The interstellar medium between stars in the Milky Way contains about one hydrogen atom per cubic centimetre on average — a vacuum so empty it would be considered impossibly rarified by any lab standard on Earth.
Molecular clouds — the densest regions of the interstellar medium — are cold (10–30 K), contain mostly molecular hydrogen (H2), and are the birthplaces of nearly all stars in the Milky Way.

Webb detected water vapour, sulfur dioxide, and sand clouds (silicate particles) in the atmosphere of exoplanet WASP-107b — providing the most detailed atmospheric chemistry of a distant world ever obtained.
The Chandra X-ray Observatory discovered that Abell 2029, one of the most massive galaxy clusters known, contains a single galaxy at its centre so large it alone spans about 6 million light-years.

The Spitzer Space Telescope discovered that the Milky Way's central bar is longer and more prominent than previously thought — stretching about 27,000 light-years and containing billions of older, redder stars.
Australia's DSN Honeysuckle Creek tracking station played a pivotal role in Apollo 11 — it relayed the clearest first footage of Neil Armstrong's first steps on the Moon to the world.

The transit of Venus across the face of the Sun — a rare event that comes in pairs separated by eight years — was used in the 18th century to calculate the distance from Earth to the Sun using parallax.
Europa's surface is crisscrossed by long dark streaks called lineae, caused by tidal flexing that cracks the ice shell; some contain materials dredged up from the subsurface ocean below.
Saturn's largest storm, the Great White Spot, erupts roughly every 29 years — approximately once per Saturnian year — wrapping entirely around the planet before dissipating.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) and ATLAS experiments at CERN, while primarily particle physics instruments, also help constrain dark matter models by searching for missing momentum in proton collision products.

The Milky Way likely swallowed a smaller galaxy called Gaia-Enceladus about 10 billion years ago — an event that contributed roughly half of the stars in the Milky Way's inner halo and thickened its disk.
TON 618 is one of the most massive known black holes — about 66 billion solar masses — and powers an ultraluminous quasar located 10.4 billion light-years away.
The mass of all the stars in the Milky Way totals only about 5% of its total mass — the rest is dark matter forming an invisible halo extending hundreds of thousands of light-years.

NASA's twin Van Allen Probes (2012–2019) discovered that Earth's inner radiation belt can almost entirely disappear after intense solar storms and rapidly reform — shedding new light on space weather dynamics.
China's Queqiao relay satellite, placed at the Earth-Moon L2 Lagrange point in 2018, enabled communications between Earth and the far side of the Moon for the Chang'e 4 and Yutu-2 missions.
Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft ever to have flown past all four outer planets — Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1981), Uranus (1986), and Neptune (1989) — on a single grand tour trajectory.

The Borisov interstellar comet, unlike 'Oumuamua, had a clearly cometary appearance with a coma and tail, and spectroscopy showed it was made of carbon monoxide ice similar to comets in our own solar system.
Tabby's Star (KIC 8462852) dims irregularly by up to 22% — far more than any planet transit could explain — and remains one of the most mysterious stellar phenomena observed by the Kepler telescope.

The Trojan asteroids at Jupiter's L4 and L5 points are so numerous they contain more mass than the entire main asteroid belt — yet they have never been visited by a spacecraft until NASA's Lucy mission.

Phosphorus, a key element for DNA and cell membranes, was recently detected in Enceladus's ocean plumes by the Cassini spacecraft — making it the first ocean world found to contain all six elements essential for life.

The IDA (Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee) has published guidelines since 1993 recommending that satellites deorbit within 25 years after mission end — yet compliance rates remain below 50%.

China plans to launch its Xuntian Space Telescope in the late 2020s — a Hubble-class instrument with a field of view 300 times larger than Hubble's that will orbit close to the Tiangong station for periodic servicing.

The ISRO-NASA NISAR satellite, planned for launch around 2025, will use dual-frequency synthetic aperture radar to map Earth's entire surface every 12 days, monitoring earthquakes, glaciers, and ecosystems.
Heat shields used on Mars entry vehicles must withstand temperatures exceeding 1,600°C during entry — Perseverance's 4.5-metre PICA-X heat shield was the largest ever flown to Mars at that time.

Curiosity rover has a nuclear power source — a multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator (MMRTG) powered by plutonium-238 decay — giving it effectively unlimited operational life regardless of dust storms or night.

Astronomers using the South Pole Telescope detected for the first time the polarised light of the cosmic microwave background being lensed by massive structures — a technique that can measure neutrino mass from space.

The Rubin Observatory will generate about 15 terabytes of data per night, discovering up to 10 million transient events and enabling real-time alerts about supernovae, asteroids, and other dynamic phenomena.

India's Aditya-L1 mission carries seven payloads to study solar wind, magnetic fields, and the solar corona simultaneously — giving Indian scientists real-time space weather data to protect satellites and infrastructure.
A parsec — the unit astronomers use for measuring stellar distances — equals 3.26 light-years, and is defined as the distance at which one astronomical unit subtends an angle of one arcsecond.

Gravitational microlensing — where a foreground star bends and brightens a background star's light — has revealed dozens of exoplanets that other methods miss, especially cold planets far from their stars.
Strontium, produced in neutron star mergers, was detected in the optical afterglow of the kilonova GW170817 — directly observing r-process nucleosynthesis for the first time.

Synchrotron radiation — emitted by electrons spiralling at nearly the speed of light around magnetic field lines — illuminates pulsars, supernova remnants, and galaxy jets, and is also harnessed in laboratory accelerators.
Barnard's Star, 5.96 light-years away, is the fastest-moving star in the sky relative to our Sun — it will be our nearest stellar neighbour in about 9,800 years before receding again.

The Faint Young Sun Paradox describes the puzzle that the early Sun was 30% less luminous than today, yet Earth was not a frozen snowball — resolved partly by higher concentrations of greenhouse gases like methane and CO2.
Astronomers using the Event Horizon Telescope have imaged the shadow of the black hole in M87 with enough resolution to resolve features the size of a golf ball on the Moon.

NASA's SOFIA (Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy), a telescope on a Boeing 747, detected oxygen in the Martian atmosphere and confirmed atomic oxygen near the lunar south pole before it was retired in 2022.

The Crab Nebula pulsar loses energy at a rate equivalent to 100,000 times the total luminosity of the Sun — all from its slowing rotation — and this spindown powers the X-ray, optical, and radio nebula around it.
Asteroid Didymos-Dimorphos was the first planetary defense target ever tested; DART's impact shifted Dimorphos's orbit by 32 minutes — more than NASA's minimum success criterion of 73 seconds.

ESA's Hera mission, launched in October 2024, will visit the Dimorphos system to measure the aftermath of the DART impact — determining the crater size, composition, and how DART changed the asteroid's interior.

The heliopause marks the outer boundary of our solar system — the point where the Sun's solar wind pressure equals the pressure of interstellar gas; both Voyager probes have now crossed this boundary.
A spacesuit for a Mars mission will need to protect against 1% of Earth's atmospheric pressure, temperatures swinging from -125°C to 20°C, intense UV radiation, and perchlorates in the Martian dust.

The Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam survey mapped 300 million galaxies to reveal the large-scale structure of the universe in unprecedented detail, finding slight tension with the standard cosmological model.

The Cosmic Infrared Background — a diffuse glow of infrared light spread across the entire sky — is produced by the combined emission of all stars and galaxies throughout cosmic history and contains information about the epoch of reionization.

The reionization epoch, roughly 150 million to 1 billion years after the Big Bang, is when the first stars and galaxies lit up and their ultraviolet light ionized the neutral hydrogen that had filled the universe.
Pluto's atmosphere is primarily nitrogen with traces of methane and carbon monoxide, and it expands as Pluto approaches the Sun and partially freezes out when Pluto moves farther away.
Pluto has red-tinted patches called tholins — complex organic molecules formed when nitrogen and methane are irradiated by solar ultraviolet light — creating its reddish, rust-coloured regions.

Saturn's north polar hexagon — a six-sided jet stream about 29,000 km across — has persisted for at least 40 years; each side is longer than Earth's diameter and it rotates with the planet's interior.
Venus's surface pressure is 92 times Earth's — equivalent to being 900 metres underwater — which crushed early Soviet landers within minutes before they could transmit data.

Uranus emits almost no internal heat — unlike all other giant planets — suggesting its internal heat transport is blocked by a stable layer in its interior created by some event, possibly an ancient giant impact.

The National Academies Planetary Science Decadal Survey 2023-2032 ranked a Uranus orbiter and probe as the highest-priority large mission for the next decade — the first dedicated mission to Uranus ever.

Neptune's moon Triton is slowly spiralling inward and will reach the Roche limit — where tidal forces will tear it apart — in approximately 3.6 billion years, possibly creating a ring system comparable to Saturn's.

Deep space optical communications (DSOC), tested by NASA's Psyche mission in 2023, demonstrated laser communication from 16 million km — achieving data rates 10–100 times faster than traditional radio links.

Cold welding — where two metal surfaces fuse in the vacuum of space without heat — was a concern for early spacecraft design and is why some mechanisms use special lubricants or non-metallic materials.
The Parker Solar Probe reached a record speed of 692,000 km/h in 2024 during its closest perihelion pass — the fastest any human-made object has ever travelled.

GJ 1132b, a rocky exoplanet 41 light-years away, may have had its original hydrogen atmosphere stripped away and a new secondary atmosphere generated by volcanic outgassing — offering a glimpse of how planets can regenerate atmospheres.

Gamma-ray burst afterglows can be detected at redshifts greater than 9 — meaning the explosion occurred when the universe was less than 500 million years old — making them cosmic lighthouses for the early universe.

Arp 87, a pair of interacting galaxies imaged by Hubble, shows a bridge of stars and gas connecting the two systems — stellar streams that will eventually merge into a single, larger galaxy over billions of years.

The South Pole-Aitken Basin on the Moon is the largest confirmed impact crater in the solar system — 2,500 km wide and 8 km deep — and its floor may contain materials from deep within the Moon's mantle.
The FAST telescope has detected over 1,000 fast radio bursts, including long-period repeating events that challenge every existing theoretical model for FRB generation.
Neutron star mergers are estimated to produce about 10 Earth-masses of gold each time — and given the estimated merger rate across the universe, these events explain why gold exists on Earth at all.

In 2022, the Webb telescope captured Jupiter in infrared, revealing its auroras, moons, and faint rings simultaneously in a single composite image — the most detailed view of the gas giant from space.
The Kuiper Belt extends from Neptune's orbit at 30 AU to about 50 AU, but a scattered disk of icy objects — flung into highly elliptical orbits by Neptune's gravity — reaches far beyond.
Centaurs are small bodies orbiting the Sun between Jupiter and Neptune with unstable orbits influenced by multiple planets — they are believed to be Kuiper Belt objects that were scattered inward.

Chiron, the first Centaur discovered (1977), was initially classified as an asteroid but was later found to display cometary activity — outgassing when it approaches the Sun — so it is classified as both.

The Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) is expected to detect 5 to 10 million asteroids and extend the known near-Earth object catalogue by an order of magnitude over its 10-year survey.
Asteroid 99942 Apophis will pass within 31,000 km of Earth on April 13, 2029 — closer than geostationary satellites — in the closest confirmed approach of an asteroid this large in recorded history.
ESA's Gaia mission discovered a population of stars in the Milky Way's disk with orbital properties suggesting they originated in the Gaia-Enceladus galaxy merger 10 billion years ago.
Oxygen-16, the most common isotope of oxygen, is forged in the cores of massive stars by helium burning; without stellar nucleosynthesis, oxygen — essential to life — would not exist in the universe.

ISRO's Space Docking Experiment (SpaDeX), launched in December 2024, tested autonomous docking technology in orbit — a critical capability for future crewed missions, lunar surface operations, and on-orbit refuelling.
China's Deep Space Exploration (Tianwen) programme plans missions to Jupiter, Uranus, and the main asteroid belt through the 2030s, as well as a comet sample-return mission.

The Chandler wobble is a small deviation in Earth's axis of rotation with a period of about 433 days; its energy source — long unexplained — is now attributed largely to fluctuations in ocean bottom pressure.

The NASA-ESA Cassini–Huygens mission revealed that Titan's rivers and lakes of liquid hydrocarbons could support exotic non-water-based life using acetylene as an energy source — a purely speculative but chemically plausible idea.
Huygens probe, released by Cassini, parachuted through Titan's thick atmosphere and landed on its surface in January 2005, transmitting 72 minutes of data including the sounds of its descent.

The Chelyabinsk meteor in February 2013 entered Earth's atmosphere at 60,000 km/h and released energy equivalent to 30 Hiroshima bombs — injuring over 1,500 people from the shockwave without hitting the ground.
The Space Shuttle programme flew 135 missions over 30 years and deployed Hubble, assembled the ISS, and carried the first American woman to space — Sally Ride in 1983 — before retiring in 2011.
The Cosmic Void — the Boötes Void — is an enormous near-empty region of space about 330 million light-years across containing almost no galaxies, one of the largest known voids in the universe.
The Sagittarius A* black hole flares in X-rays multiple times per day as gas clouds and small objects fall into its accretion zone — Chandra and XMM-Newton have monitored these flares for decades.
Magnetic reconnection — the explosive realignment of magnetic field lines in plasma — is responsible for solar flares, Earth's auroras, and particle acceleration in pulsars and black hole jets.

The Hubble Space Telescope was initially returning blurry images due to a 2.2-micrometre error in its primary mirror; Space Shuttle astronauts installed corrective optics during a 1993 servicing mission, restoring it to full capability.

The Higgs boson, discovered at CERN in 2012, gives elementary particles their mass through the Higgs field — a discovery that completed the Standard Model of particle physics, which also underlies our understanding of the Big Bang.
The Sun is classified as a G-type main-sequence star (G2V) — a yellow dwarf — though it appears white from space; about 10% of Milky Way stars are solar-type or cooler G-type stars.
Red dwarf stars — M-type stars — are the most common type in the galaxy (about 70% of all stars), yet they burn so slowly they can live for tens to hundreds of billions of years.

The Gliese 581 system, a red dwarf 20 light-years away, was one of the first to be found harbouring multiple exoplanets in or near the habitable zone, sparking early excitement about nearby potentially Earth-like worlds.

Space-based solar power — collecting sunlight in geostationary orbit and beaming microwave energy to receivers on Earth — has been studied since the 1970s and is now being actively prototyped by ESA and several national agencies.

Earth's magnetosphere protects life from the solar wind by deflecting most charged particles; without it — as on Mars, which lost its magnetosphere billions of years ago — the atmosphere would slowly erode away.

The Moon's surface is covered by regolith — a fine, powdery layer of broken rock and glass produced by billions of years of micrometeorite impacts — and future lunar bases may use it as raw material for construction.
Lunar lava tubes — collapsed or intact tunnels left by ancient volcanic flows — could provide natural radiation-shielded habitats for future lunar settlers, some estimated to be kilometres wide.

ESA's LISA Pathfinder mission (2015–2017) demonstrated laser interferometry in space with 1,000 times better precision than required — paving the way for the full LISA gravitational wave observatory in the 2030s.

In-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) — using local materials on the Moon or Mars to make propellant, oxygen, and building materials — is considered essential to making long-term off-Earth settlements economically viable.
The Goldbach-Mandel observation of a stellar occultation by Triton in 1989 revealed its thin nitrogen atmosphere — a discovery made from Earth just months before Voyager 2 flew past Neptune.
